Negative feelings about life are more common among teens on Instagram and TikTok | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A recent survey of teenagers suggests that a large portion of young people encounter negative experiences on the internet, and the types of harm they face tend to vary depending on which apps they use. The research indicates that while some issues like bullying occur at similar rates in person and online, teenagers are much more likely to be exposed to violent imagery or unwanted sexual content through digital platforms. The findings were published in JAMA Pediatrics.

The term “online harms” refers to a wide range of negative experiences on digital platforms, such as cyberbullying, unwanted sexual advances, or exposure to content that encourages self-injury. Prior studies have demonstrated that digital platforms host a variety of risks for adolescents.

For example, a 2022 survey study found that different types of online sexual abuse, such as nonconsensual sexting or grooming by adults, occur at varying rates among youth. Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 indicated that nearly half of adolescents who send sexually explicit images experience nonconsensual sharing or extortion.

Most existing research tends to examine one specific type of negative experience at a time, such as harassment, rather than capturing the full spectrum of issues adolescents face. When studies do measure these risks, they rarely break the numbers down by specific platforms to see how experiences might differ on an app like TikTok compared to an app like YouTube. To explore this, research covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that short-form video apps are associated with more severe body image concerns, suggesting that specific app designs might play a role in user well-being.

The research, led by Angela Y. Lee, an assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s School of Journalism and Mass Communication who was a postdoctoral fellow at Stanford Medicine’s Center for Digital Health when the study was conducted, aimed to estimate how often adolescents report various negative experiences both online and offline. “This study was the product of a great collaboration of researchers from Stanford, USC, NYU, and UW-Madison, working across psychology, communication, medicine, technology policy, and consumer science,” Lee told PsyPost.

“There are widespread concerns about youth online safety and recent steps, like social media bans and age-gating policies, have been recently implemented around the world,” Lee noted. “At the same time, there are ongoing debates about how people interpret the research on social media’s effects on youth psychological well-being, and what kinds of interventions should be implemented.”

By tracking how these experiences differ across twenty popular communication platforms, the researchers hoped to demonstrate a method for gathering platform-specific data that could inform targeted prevention efforts.

“This study was motivated by something that I feel is a common goal across researchers across the aisle and policymakers, which is a need for clear, consistent, and granular measurement of youth’s online experiences,” Lee explained. “Our team’s hope is that knowing how often teens report having negative experiences on specific platforms can help add specificity to conversations about social media and well-being effects, and inform efforts to track if interventions that are implemented are meaningfully reducing reported harms.”

To conduct the study, the researchers used a nationally representative, probability-based sample of 472 adolescents in the United States between the ages of 13 and 17. The survey was administered between February and December 2025. Participants answered questions about their use of 20 online communication platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube, over the previous four weeks.

The survey asked the teenagers to report whether they had encountered specific negative experiences either offline or across the various platforms they used. These experiences included direct harassment, witnessing harassment, receiving unwanted sexual images, encountering violent content, seeing content that encouraged self-harm, and experiencing sleep disruption due to technology use. The research team then applied statistical weights to the data to ensure the results accurately reflected the broader population of adolescents in the United States.

The results indicated that exposure to negative experiences is common among teenagers. Across both online and offline contexts, 44.7% of the adolescents had witnessed someone else being harassed, and 29.8% reported experiencing direct harassment themselves within the four-week window. Interestingly, direct harassment was reported at similar rates offline (18.5%) and online (16.4%), suggesting that this type of conflict happens across all areas of a teenager’s life.

For other types of harm, the internet proved to be a much more common source of exposure than the offline world. The teenagers reported seeing violent imagery online at a rate of 10.7%, compared to just 1.6% offline. Similarly, 13.4% of respondents encountered unwanted sexual images online, while only 2.0% experienced this offline. Content encouraging self-harm was seen by 9.7% of adolescents online, compared to 5.2% offline. Additionally, over half of the participants (51.5%) reported that their technology use disrupted their sleep.

The study also found substantial variations depending on the specific platforms the adolescents were using. For instance, 9.1% of Instagram users reported seeing violent imagery, compared to just 1.9% of YouTube users. The feeling that one’s life is worse because of other people’s posts was most common on Instagram (16.6%) and TikTok (13.4%), while it was much lower on YouTube (4.1%) and text messaging (5.6%).

Sleep disruption also seemed to be concentrated on certain apps. A total of 42.2% of TikTok users and 27.8% of Instagram users attributed their disrupted sleep to those platforms. In comparison, only 10.2% of teenagers blamed text messaging for their sleep issues.

The researchers noted that factors like parental education, household income, and the presence of parental controls on smartphones were not statistically associated with a higher or lower likelihood of experiencing online harm.

As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, the study relies on a relatively modest sample size of 472 adolescents. When looking at less popular platforms or rare experiences, the small number of users limits how precise the estimates can be.

“Although this is a nationally representative sample of American teens, it’s a relatively small sample and this was a pilot study,” Lee said. “The results should not be taken to say definitively that X platform has Y amount of harms, but rather can be thought of as illustrating how reported harms vary from platform to platform and from harm to harm. We do hope to be quite clear that this is a pilot!”

Second, the findings are based on self-reported memories over a four-week period. This approach is subject to recall bias, meaning teenagers might be more likely to remember highly emotional events while forgetting milder, everyday interactions. Stigmatized events, such as receiving or sending explicit images, might also be underreported due to social desirability or embarrassment.

Another detail to consider is that adolescents might simply attribute their negative experiences to the apps they spend the most time on, rather than the exact place the harm occurred. Because teenagers often use multiple apps at once, it can be difficult for them to pinpoint exactly where they saw a distressing video or received a hurtful message.

Finally, the differences in reported harms across platforms might reflect the types of people who choose to use those apps, rather than just the design of the apps themselves. For instance, if a specific platform is highly popular among teenage girls, who generally report higher susceptibility to social comparison, that app might show elevated rates of body image concerns regardless of its layout or content moderation policies.

“This is cross-sectional survey data, so it cannot be used to draw causal claims,” Lee added. “We can’t say that ‘using platform X causes American teens to see unwanted content Y’ but we can say that adolescents using platform X were more likely to report seeing content Y. We also do not know what the effects of such reported harms are on youth well-being, though that is something we hope to address in future research.”

Future research using larger samples could help clarify how specific platform features directly influence user experiences.

“In the near future, we’re in the process of preparing to field a new, larger study with American adolescents and their parents that will allow us to examine how youth report experiencing online harms across a broader set of platforms – including AI chatbots and AI companion apps,” she said. “We think this next step is important because the digital landscape of youth media use is changing rapidly, and measurement efforts need to keep up to understand where, when, and how youth are being negatively impacted.”

“Long-term, I am hopeful that studies like ours – and those conducted by nonprofit and academic entities – can show that investment in monitoring youth online experiences can provide valuable insights that can help inform efforts to implement and evaluate interventions,” Lee concluded.

The Patent: US20090062677A1

Title: "Method of Recording and Saving of Human Soul for Human Immortality and Installation for it"

Inventor: Alexander Alexandrovich Bolonkin, Brooklyn, NY

Filed: December 20, 2006

Published: March 5, 2009

Legal Status: Abandoned

What the Patent Actually Says

The abstract is explicit: "The inventor shows that a human soul is only the information in human brain. He offers a method for re-writing the human brain on electronic chips. This method allows for the modeling of a human soul in order to achieve man immortality. This method does not damage the brain but works to extend and enhance it."

The patent describes a wearable recording system including:

◾ A micro video camera positioned at the head to record everything the person sees
◾ A microphone to record everything the person says and hears
◾ Body sensors to record physical conditions: eye opening, body temperature, blood pressure, heart palpitations, skin resistance, perspiration, skin temperature, respiration activity, pain, and more
◾ Navigation systems to record body position on Earth
◾ A portable computer (chip) and portable memory carried on the body
◾ Long-term high-capacity memory for periodic rewriting of the recorded data

The patent explicitly frames the human soul as information nothing more. It claims that by recording every sensory input, every physical state, and every moment of a person's life, you can create a model of the soul that can be saved eternally.

The Inventor: Alexander Bolonkin

Alexander Bolonkin was a Soviet-era aerospace engineer and scientist who immigrated to the United States. His patent is not the work of a fringe figure he holds multiple patents and published extensively on topics ranging from space technology to human immortality. His later writings explicitly describe his goal as creating an "E-Substance" (E-существо) an electronic human and he argued that the goal of mankind's existence is to create the "Supreme Mind" and keep it forever.

This is the transhumanist vision in its rawest form: the belief that human consciousness is merely data, that the body is a shell, and that immortality can be achieved by uploading the "soul" onto a machine.

The Legal Status: "Abandoned" Is Not "Harmless"

The patent was abandoned. That means Bolonkin did not pursue it to grant. But abandonment does not erase the filing. The document is a matter of public record. It proves that the concept was formally proposed, legally documented, and entered into the global patent system.

The question: if this was filed in 2006, where has the technology reached now, two decades later?

The Broader Pattern: This Is Not an Isolated Patent

The Bolonkin patent is part of a documented lineage of similar filings:

◾ US 2012/0136403 A1  "Medically Perpetual Persistence of Essential Human Life" describes transferring memory and consciousness from one brain to another, including across clones
◾US 20250258545A1 (2025)  "3D Digital Immortality And Uses Thereof" describes copying thoughts and memories into a computer to create digital emulations of human brains
◾ Meta's patent US-12513102-B2 filed in 2023 and published in 2026 describes using large language models to simulate a deceased user's social media activity, effectively creating a digital version of the person that continues posting after death
◾Microsoft's "deceased chatbot" patent validated in 2021, describes creating a chatbot based on a specific person, potentially a deceased loved one
◾ Whole brain emulation patents including US12536425B1, which describes a system for generating a simulated humanoid based on brain data

This is not one inventor's fantasy. This is a research direction, a sustained, multi-decade, multi-company effort to develop the technology to capture, store, and transfer human consciousness.

The Transhumanist Agenda: The WEF and the Elite

The World Economic Forum has made no secret of its transhumanist ambitions:

◾Klaus Schwab, in a leaked video from a private WEF session, promised recruits that their "avatar" will continue to live after they die and that their brains "will be replicated through artificial intelligence and algorithms"
◾Yuval Noah Harari, a WEF advisor, has publicly stated that human rights are a fiction and that the future belongs to a bio-engineered, AI-networked "god-like" species that will render the old, organic human obsolete
◾Elon Musk, at Davos, declared that aging "is a very solvable problem" and that Neuralink is working on brain-computer interfaces that could one day allow people to "store your memories"
◾The WEF's "Great Reset" explicitly calls for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, which includes AI, the Internet of Things, and the integration of human biology with digital systems

The vision is consistent: the human being is data, the body is obsolete, and immortality is achievable through technology.

The Satanic Dimension

The transhumanist project is not merely technological. It is theological. It is a direct assault on the foundational claims of every spiritual tradition:

◾ It denies that the soul is a divine spark, a gift from the Creator, a sacred and irreducible essence. It reduces the soul to information data to be recorded, copied, and stored.
◾ It denies that death is a transition, a return to the Source, or a doorway to the next life. It reframes death as a technical problem to be solved by engineering.
◾It denies that the human being is made in the image of God. It proposes that the human being is made in the image of the machine and that the machine is superior.
◾ It seeks to replace the Creator with the created. The "Supreme Mind" of Bolonkin's writings is not God. It is an artificial intelligence built by human hands, worshipped as the new god.

This is the same inversion we have seen throughout the control grid: the sacred is profaned, the profane is sanctified, and the human being is reduced to a commodity. The soul becomes data. The body becomes a vessel. Death becomes a bug. And the machine becomes the god.

How to Verify This Yourself

You do not need to trust me or anyone else. The evidence is publicly available:

1. Google Patents: Search for US20090062677A1. The full patent text, drawings, and legal status are available for free.
2. USPTO: Search for the application number 11/613,380.
3. Related patents: Search for US20120136403A1, US20250258545A1, and US12536425B1 to see the broader pattern.
4. WEF publications: Search for the WEF's "Fourth Industrial Revolution" and Yuval Harari's statements on human obsolescence.
5. Neuralink: Review Neuralink's own public statements about memory storage and brain-computer interfaces.

The Final Truth

The patent is real. The technology is real. The agenda is real. The legal status of "abandoned" does not mean the idea was discarded, it means the specific application was not pursued. The concept has been absorbed, refined, and advanced by other inventors, other companies, and other institutions.

The question is not whether they are working on this. The question is how far they have gotten, and what they plan to do with it when it is complete.

Excited to share 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗘𝘃𝗼-𝗩𝗟, our new work on on-policy self-distillation for multimodal model self-improvement!

The motivation is simple: as generation and understanding come together in multimodal systems, models can provide feedback on their own outputs. Can that feedback become a useful training signal—turning their ability to evaluate into improvements in generation?

📈 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀

Building on Qwen-image-2512, UniEvo-VL improves:

• GenEval: 𝟬.𝟳𝟰𝟳 → 𝟬.𝟴𝟬𝟴
• GenEval2 Soft-TIFA: 𝟯𝟮.𝟵𝟳 → 𝟯𝟱.𝟱𝟯
These gains show the potential of learning from self-generated feedback. But the boundaries are just as interesting.

🔍 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴?

Experiments with stronger external critics suggest room for further improvement.

This raises a central challenge: producing feedback is only the beginning. That feedback must be reliable enough to guide learning. Understanding what makes a good critic matters for building a better generator.

🔍 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀?

Not uniformly. Text-rendering results remain mixed, even as the overall generation benchmarks improve.

Progress on one benchmark does not mean every capability improves alongside it—a useful boundary to understand when studying self-improving systems.

For me, the broader research question is:

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹’𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲?

UniEvo-VL takes a step toward answering this question for multimodal generation, exploring both the opportunities and the limitations.

A reward of “3” can mean two completely different things.
Everyone thinks a response is mediocre — or half the people love it while the other half hate it.
Most Reward Models cannot tell the difference.
Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM): instead of collapsing human preference into a single score, DRM learns the full reward distribution, preserving disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments.
✨ Paper:https://t.co/wS1fmHBeRV  
🤗 Models: https://t.co/RGTU759A5y  
💻 GitHub: https://t.co/KAow6DcoNn

Why it matters:
Human disagreement is structured, not just noise. On datasets with repeated annotations, judgments often form separated or polarized patterns. More importantly, as human disagreement increases, DRM’s learned reward distribution becomes increasingly multimodal.

The distribution is useful, not just descriptive. DRM can use distributional uncertainty to identify unstable reward decisions, and distribution-aware ranking improves Best-of-N selection beyond simply taking the mean reward.

Reward Models get their own test-time scaling. Instead of only spending more compute on generating more responses, DRM can keep the response fixed and sample its reward distribution more times. More reward samples give a more reliable estimate — a new scaling axis unavailable to deterministic scalar RMs.

And the gains survive RLHF. When used as the training-time reward, DRM improves downstream policy performance over scalar reward baselines, showing that the benefit is not limited to offline RM benchmarks.

The takeaway: Reward modeling may lose something important when it compresses every human judgment into one number.
“Everyone thinks this is average” and “people strongly disagree about this” should not look identical to a Reward Model.
DRM makes that difference visible — and usable.

Excited to share that our paper "ParetoSlider: Diffusion Models Post-Training for Continuous Reward Control" has been accepted to @NeurIPSConf as an oral! 🎉

ParetoSlider enables continuous inference-time control over competing reward trade-offs with a single diffusion model, without retraining or maintaining multiple checkpoints.
